subject: Critical Thinking
title: The Fallacy Fallacy: Calling Out Errors Incorrectly
description: A quick win: understand The Fallacy Fallacy: Calling Out Errors Incorrectly.

hook.text: 'You used an ad hominem! Therefore your conclusion is wrong!' That itself is a fallacy. Welcome to the meta-level.

buildup.text: The fallacy fallacy: assuming a conclusion is false because the argument for it contains a fallacy.

discovery.text: Bad arguments can reach true conclusions. 'The sky is blue because unicorns said so' — bad reasoning, true conclusion.

twist.text: Internet debates are plagued by this. People cry 'fallacy!' as if naming it disproves the claim. It doesn't.

climax.text: The proper response to a fallacy is 'Your reasoning is flawed' — not 'Your conclusion is wrong.'

punchline.text: Finding a bad argument isn't the same as proving it wrong.

quiz.question: What is the fallacy fallacy?
options: Assuming a conclusion is false because the argument for it is fallacious
Using too many fallacies at once

details.summary: The fallacy fallacy assumes that because an argument contains a fallacy, its conclusion must be false. A flawed argument can still reach a true conclusion. Fallacy detection tells you the argument is bad, not that the claim is wrong.
details.whyItMatters: Using fallacy detection as an automatic truth detector is itself a reasoning error. Bad arguments can support true conclusions, and dismissing them entirely is intellectually lazy.
takeaways: A fallacious argument can still have a true conclusion
Identifying a fallacy weakens the argument, not the claim itself
You still need to evaluate the claim on its independent merits

faq.question: How should you respond when you spot a fallacy in someone's argument?
faq.answer: Point out the flaw in the reasoning but then evaluate the conclusion independently. The claim might be true for reasons the person did not articulate. Dismissing the conclusion solely because of the fallacy is itself a fallacy.

faq.question: Is the fallacy fallacy commonly used in online debates?
faq.answer: Yes. People who learn about fallacies sometimes use them as weapons to dismiss arguments entirely rather than engaging the substance. Naming a fallacy becomes a shortcut to avoid the harder work of evaluating the actual claim.
